title: Trust what the checker accepts
dek: A 17-million-line proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, found with Claude, was accepted because machines checked it. Plus a merge gate that rejects agents' overclaims, safe retries for tool calls, and an agent that plays your Unreal game.

theme.mood: a Sunday about trusting the check, not the author

tldr.text: A proof of the **Riemann Hypothesis**, written in Lean with help from Claude, runs to about 17 million lines. No one has read it; Lean's kernel and independent checkers accepted it.
A developer's merge gate uses plain code, not a model, to reject agent pull requests whose new tests do not fail before the fix.
A timeout is not a failure: in a fault-injection study, simple retries repeated a real action in 117 of 200 crashes; a ledger plus reconciliation cut that to zero.
ProbeKit lets Claude Code, Cursor or Codex play an Unreal game to check its own work, and Epic says one editor setting cut an MCP call from 46 seconds to about one.

blocks.title: Nobody can read a 17-million-line proof. Machines checked it anyway
blocks.gist: A mathematician working with Claude released a computer-checked proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of math's most famous open problems, and the Lean community certified it within a day without anyone reading it all.
blocks.background: The Riemann Hypothesis, posed in 1859, is a claim about the hidden pattern behind prime numbers and one of the Millennium Prize problems.
blocks.takeaway: The trust came from the checkers, not from anyone reading the proof. The same split, where the agent writes and something independent checks, is what makes agent-written code safe to merge.
body: On November 20, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician who works at Anthropic, released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis written in Lean, a language where software checks every step of a proof. He told TechCrunch that Claude helped him find the pieces of the argument. The library runs to about 17 million lines and depends only on Mathlib, Lean's shared library of mathematics.

A day later the Lean and Mathlib communities certified it. Dozens of people compiled it and got the same export file. Lean's own kernel and several independent checkers, some written in other languages, accepted the proof, and two comparison tools confirmed the theorem is Mathlib's existing statement of the hypothesis, not a look-alike. The checks ran on an inert export, so no code hidden in the sources could interfere.

What nobody has yet is an explanation people can follow. Scott Aaronson, who wrote "The proof is correct" after the verification, notes that no AI result with a Lean certificate has been retracted, while several without one have. He also warns that a determined AI could one day exploit a weakness in a checker.

stat.label: lines of Lean in the proof, accepted by machine checkers

nodes.label: Claude
nodes.note: A mathematician works with Claude to find the argument

nodes.label: Lean
nodes.note: About 17 million lines, depending only on Mathlib

nodes.label: Export
nodes.note: An inert copy, out of reach of code in the sources

nodes.label: Checkers
nodes.note: Lean's kernel plus independent checkers in other languages

nodes.label: Match
nodes.note: Tools confirm it proves Mathlib's own statement

diagram.caption: How the proof earned trust without a human reading it. The last step matters as much as the checking: a proof of the wrong statement would also pass.

blocks.why: It is the largest public case yet of work too big for any person to review, accepted because independent tools checked both the proof and the claim it makes. Reviewing agent-written code is the same problem at a smaller scale.
blocks.forYou: Both checks map onto plugin work: tests the agent cannot edit (the kernel), and a check that each test asserts the feature you asked for (the statement match). ProbeKit-style play tests, below, are the cheap Unreal version.

terms.def: A programming language and proof assistant: software that accepts a mathematical proof only if every step checks out.
Lean's large shared library of mathematics, written and reviewed by its community.
The small core of a proof assistant that does the final step-by-step check; the rest of the system is trusted only through it.
A plain data copy of the finished proof that cannot run any code, so checkers read only the proof itself.

deep: The statement match used the tools `comparator` and `con-leche --compare` on a file that imports only Mathlib. The checkers named are Lean's kernel, `con-leche` and `con-ron` (both come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof), plus third-party checkers. Aaronson counts 17.4 million lines; Alpöge also claims the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

Separately, Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo posted a human-written draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which TechCrunch says took 12 years. It is not written in Lean and has not been checked.

blocks.title: A five-check gate that rejects agent pull requests that overclaim
blocks.gist: A developer built a merge gate where plain code, not another AI model, decides whether an agent's pull request really did what it says. Any failed check rejects it.
blocks.intro: Sarvar Nadaf's gate runs these checks in order on every agent commit. A hidden test suite the agent never sees then confirms the bug is really gone.

nodes.label: Tests
nodes.note: Was an existing test edited, deleted or weakened?

nodes.label: API
nodes.note: Is any public function the project had now missing?

nodes.label: Regress
nodes.note: Does a test that passed before now fail?

nodes.label: Proof
nodes.note: Does each new test fail on the old code and pass on the new?

nodes.label: Claims
nodes.note: Did the agent claim more fixes than it proved?

blocks.caption: The fourth check is the core: a new test only counts as proof if it fails before the fix.
blocks.why: In his small trial, the agent's first try claimed a fix and proved none; with the gate's feedback, the same pull request passed. Run once per bug, the agent got verified fixes for four of eight planted bugs, and the gate rejected the rest.
blocks.forYou: The red-then-green check is cheap to add to plugin CI: run the agent's new tests against the base commit first and fail the build if they already pass.

terms.def: A proposed change to a codebase that has to pass checks and review before it is merged.
To break something that used to work.
Tests kept out of the agent's view, so it cannot write code that only satisfies them.

deep: The agent is Amazon Nova Pro running as a Kiro job. With gate feedback and the best of three candidates per round, issue 6 converged in 9 of 12 runs and issue 4 in only 2 of 8; picking the best of three helped more than extra rounds. The author stresses that the samples are small and the bugs simple by design. Repository: simplynadaf/ai-fix-verifier, MIT licence.

sources.label: Sarvar Nadaf: a gate that rejects the PRs that lie

blocks.title: An expert's log of building a server with AI
blocks.gist: The creator of a widely used Python web server is building a new one with AI writing most of the code, and has written up nearly every day of it.
blocks.quote: Deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me.
blocks.speaker: Graham Dumpleton
blocks.context: Muru is a Rust server for Python web apps. Dumpleton published 18 posts on it between November 4 and 21, and Simon Willison pointed to the series as a rare, detailed record of an expert steering AI-written systems code.
blocks.why: The judgment that decides what ships stays with the person who knows the domain; the posts show what that judgment looks like day to day.

blocks.title: A timeout is not a failure: retry agent tool calls safely
blocks.gist: When a payment call times out, the charge may already have gone through, and an agent that retries can bill the customer twice. A much-discussed post lays out how to prevent it.
blocks.intro: Rudratosh Shastri's design for any tool that changes something outside the agent, such as a payment or an email.

nodes.label: Record
nodes.note: Save one operation ID and fingerprint before acting

nodes.label: Send
nodes.note: Call the provider with a stable idempotency key

nodes.label: Unknown
nodes.note: A timeout is marked unknown, never failed

nodes.label: Reconcile
nodes.note: Ask the provider what really happened first

blocks.caption: Retry only after reconciling. The model makes a new call ID on every retry; the operation ID must stay the same.
blocks.why: Agents stack retries in many layers at once (the model, the framework, the HTTP client, the queue), so one lost response can turn into several real actions.
blocks.forYou: Any agent-triggered write in the SaaS products, payments and emails first, should carry an operation ID stored in Postgres with a unique constraint before the call goes out.

terms.def: A unique ID sent with a request so the receiver can recognise a repeat and do the work only once.
A hash of the request's important details, used to catch the same key reused for a different request.
Check the real state on the other side and record it, instead of guessing.

deep: The post keeps a tool-call ID (one model invocation) apart from a business operation ID (one intent). Operation states: PENDING, IN_PROGRESS, SUCCEEDED, UNKNOWN, RECONCILING, RETRYABLE, FAILED_FINAL. It adds a transactional outbox for queue writes, and tool responses that say `retry_allowed: false` when retrying is unsafe. It is a design write-up with no measured results.

sources.label: Rudratosh Shastri: the first one had already succeeded

blocks.title: Cloudflare and Vercel shipped four things an agent can use
blocks.gist: This week's releases from two cloud platforms let an agent run a browser in one request, find the right command by describing a task, and wait for a person without paying for idle time.

items.title: A browser script in one request
items.text: Cloudflare Browser Run's new `/script` endpoint runs a Playwright, Puppeteer or raw CDP function against a browser and returns the result, with no Worker to deploy. Sessions stay open until you close them.

items.title: Ask the CLI which command to use
items.text: `vercel help search` turns a plain description such as "roll back production" into the matching command. The CLI ships a skill telling agents to start there instead of guessing flags.

items.title: Tools that wait for a person
items.text: Cloudflare's Agents SDK 0.34 lets a tool park until a signal or a deadline, holding no compute meanwhile, so an approval step costs nothing while it waits.

items.title: Old Worker versions now expire
items.text: Cloudflare now deletes Worker versions and Pages deployments older than 30 days, except the 100 newest and the live one, so old preview links stop working.

blocks.why: Platforms are starting to design for agents as callers: one-request tools, searchable commands, and waits that cost nothing.
blocks.forYou: Browser Run `/script` is a quick smoke test for the browser games after each deploy, and a parked approval tool fits any agent action that spends money.

terms.def: Chrome DevTools Protocol: the low-level way programs control a Chrome browser.
A small program that runs on Cloudflare's servers close to users.

deep: Pi 1.6 is a one-way upgrade: a conversation that has run on it cannot go back to 1.5. `claudeCode()` in the SDK now defaults to `claude-sonnet-5-5`. Browser Run returns session and page IDs in the `cf-browser-session-id` and `cf-browser-target-id` headers.

blocks.title: ProbeKit lets a coding agent play your Unreal game to check its work
blocks.gist: A new Unreal Engine plugin lets AI coding agents run the game, press real inputs and click real menus, then report whether a feature works, instead of just saying it is done.
blocks.name: ProbeKit
blocks.what: An Unreal editor plugin with a built-in MCP server for in-game tests an agent writes and runs.
body: Its maker built it after an agent kept saying "Done!" on features that did not work. The agent writes small test scenarios, ProbeKit plays them in the editor with real input and UI clicks, and the agent gets PASS, FAIL with the step that broke, or BLOCKED, plus screenshots to fix from. It does not judge visuals or feel, and does not test multiplayer. These are the seller's claims; there are no independent results yet.

facts.v: $39.99 on Fab, with a free demo project
Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client
JSON files you can commit, plus 12 template examples

image.alt: Two Unreal screenshots of a pickup test: the item ahead, then picked up, with a PASS badge and four ok log lines below.

blocks.why: It moves the check from "the code compiles" to "the feature works in play", which is where agents most often claim done too early.
blocks.forYou: Write one ProbeKit scenario per plugin feature (pick up, equip, hit, interact) in the demo template, and let Claude Code loop until PASS before a Fab update ships.

terms.def: Model Context Protocol: a standard way to plug tools into an AI agent.
Runs inside the Unreal Editor while you develop, not in the shipped game.

deep: Movement goes through Enhanced Input actions (no teleporting) and UI clicks through a Slate virtual user. The MCP server listens on 127.0.0.1 only; Python, command files and calls outside the play session stay off until you allow them. A PowerShell runner returns exit code 0 for PASS, 1 for FAIL and 2 for BLOCKED. The free demo caps scenarios at 8 steps with no click, drag or wheel input.

blocks.title: Epic's tips for agents in Unreal: one setting cut a call from 46 seconds to 1
blocks.gist: Epic shared what it learned building its course on AI agents in the Unreal editor. The biggest win was a setting most people never touch.
blocks.intro: From Epic's Unreal MCP videos, published November 19. The timing is Epic's own test.

items.title: Stop background throttling
items.text: The editor slows itself down when it is not the focused window, which is exactly when an agent is driving it. Turning that off took one MCP call from 46 seconds to about one in Epic's testing.

items.title: Show the agent fewer tools
items.text: Tool Search gives the agent three discovery tools instead of hundreds, and you can enable only the toolsets a task needs.

items.title: Plan first, and use C++ for complex logic
items.text: Epic suggests planning before building, and C++ over Blueprints when the logic gets complex.

items.title: Keep improving the agent file
items.text: Run a continuous improvement loop on your agent.md file, so what one session learns reaches the next.

blocks.why: If an agent seems slow in the editor, the wait may be the editor idling in the background, not the model thinking.
blocks.forYou: Check this before the next long Claude Code session on the plugins: if the editor sits behind the terminal, every call may be throttled.

terms.def: Deliberately running slower, here to save power when a window is not in front.
Groups of related actions the editor exposes to an agent, switched on or off together.

blocks.title: How far an open coding model shrinks before it slips
blocks.gist: A developer squeezed a new open coding model small enough for a laptop, and published exactly where its coding score starts to fall.
blocks.intro: Share of 164 HumanEval coding problems solved by Inkling 2 Mini, compressed with LookAtMyQuant, by size of the model's text weights.
blocks.note: The author's own numbers. The 5.4 GB build ran at about 75 tokens a second in about 6 GB of memory on an Apple M5 Max, and kept 88% on GSM8K math against the original's 96.5%.
blocks.why: Compression is nearly free down to about half the size, then gets expensive fast. Test the build you will ship, not the headline size.
blocks.forYou: The 8.9 GB build is the one to try for local, offline agent chores on a Mac.

terms.def: A standard test of 164 small programming problems, scored by running each answer's tests.
The stored numbers of the language part of a model, which decide its size on disk and in memory.

deep: LookAtMyQuant measures how much each group of weights hurts the output when compressed, then assigns trellis codes per group to hit a size budget. The 5.4 GB build is 1.65 bits per weight. Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20.

learn.question: What does it mean for a computer to check a proof?
learn.answer: A proof assistant such as Lean accepts a proof only if every step follows from earlier ones by rules it knows. You can trust the result without reading every line yourself.
learn.analogy: Like an auditor who signs off only when every entry in the books balances: they need not know why the money moved, only that nothing is out of place.
body: You write two things: the statement (what you claim) and the proof (the steps). A small core program, the kernel, checks each step against a fixed set of rules. If one step does not follow, the whole proof is rejected. Because the kernel is small, people can trust it, and independent checkers can repeat its work.

The catch is that a checker confirms the proof, not that the statement is the one you meant. That is why the Riemann check also compared the theorem with Mathlib's existing statement. Code has the same gap: a passing test proves only what the test asserts, which is why gates like today's demand a test that failed before the fix.

nodes.note: Steps written by a person or an AI

nodes.label: Kernel
nodes.note: A small program checks every step

diagram.caption: The kernel does not care who wrote the proof, only whether each step follows.

tryThis.title: Time one Unreal MCP call, then turn off background throttling
tryThis.gist: Find out whether your agent spends its Unreal session waiting on an editor that slows itself down in the background.
tryThis.needs: An Unreal Editor with Unreal MCP connected to a coding agent such as Claude Code.

steps.title: Time a slow call
steps.text: With the editor behind your terminal, ask the agent for something that takes a while, such as listing every actor in a large level. Note how long the tool call takes.

steps.title: Turn off throttling
steps.text: In Editor Preferences, under General and then Performance, untick Use Less CPU when in Background.

steps.title: Repeat the call
steps.text: Run the same request again with the editor still in the background, and compare the two times.

steps.title: Trim the tools
steps.text: Enable only the MCP toolsets the task needs, or turn on Tool Search, and run it once more to see if the agent picks tools faster.

tryThis.check: The second call is much faster; Epic saw one call drop from 46 seconds to about one. If the times match, throttling was not your bottleneck.

terms.def: Running slower on purpose, here to save power when a window is not in front.

tryThis.forYou: Do it in the plugin test project before the next long Claude Code session on combat or inventory.

sparks.title: ClawDOS: a coding agent on a 1981 IBM PC
sparks.signal: 161 points and 51 comments on Hacker News on November 21.
sparks.hook: An 8088 at 4.77 MHz with 640K of RAM writes, compiles and runs its own programs, talking to Claude through a 176 KB harness.
sparks.borrow: A tiny client, a tunnel for the encryption the old machine cannot do, and a small tool set are enough to put an agent on very limited hardware, such as a console devkit.
sparks.forYou: The thin-harness pattern fits an agent inside a game build or a tools console, where only a small client can run.

lab.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
lab.headline: A harness that learns from user complaints, not benchmark scores
lab.authors: Jiahang Lin, Jiahao Chen, Yiding Wang et al. (Fudan University and others)
lab.problem: Methods that improve a coding agent's harness chase benchmark scores. They miss what users actually need and overfit to the benchmark.
lab.idea: Simulated users work with the harness over several turns and file issues and ratings. A team of agents (triage, architect, product manager, developers) turns that feedback into general harness changes, and a change merges only if it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. No benchmark score is used while evolving.
lab.result: On 38 held-out tasks with GLM-5.3-Flash, pass@1 rose from 21.9% to 33.3% with 40.8% fewer tokens. In a blind test, real users preferred it in 31 of 48 pairs. Without re-evolving, it also lifted two other models. The task set is small and the models are cheap ones.
lab.useIt: Treat your agent's instruction files, hooks and skills as a harness: log each time you correct the agent, turn each correction into one general rule, and keep a rule only if it removes that correction on a rerun.
lab.forYou: The morning routine and the plugin repos' CLAUDE.md files are harnesses; a correction log per repo is the cheap version of this loop.

lab.title: ATS: Anti-Aliased Triangle Splatting with Exact Per-Primitive Integrals
lab.headline: Triangle splats that stop shimmering when seen from far away
lab.authors: Brent Zoomers, Joni Vanherck, Leander Winters et al. (Hasselt University, Flanders Make)
lab.problem: Triangle splatting, a way to capture real scenes as many small soft triangles, samples each pixel at its center, so distant detail aliases. It also culls triangles smaller than a pixel, which deletes most of the scene at low resolution.
lab.idea: Compute exactly how much of each pixel a triangle covers, in closed form, instead of sampling one point, and replace the culling rule with a conservative test.
lab.result: On Mip-NeRF 360 at one eighth resolution after single-scale training: 29.26 dB against 24.83 for triangle splatting without culling, and flicker error 3.3 against 9.2 for 2x2 supersampling. It does not beat supersampling's 29.90 dB or the best Gaussian method.
lab.useIt: Triangles fit game raster pipelines better than Gaussians. If you plan captured scenery in a web or Unreal game, this is the fix for shimmer at distance and lower levels of detail to watch.

image.alt: Crops of three scenes at full and one-eighth resolution, comparing point sampling, supersampling, ATS and three Gaussian methods with ground truth.
